catalog_quote: [Winfield 1928 p.10-11] 4. Accent. The accent or stress in a word generally falls upon the root, no matter what additions are made to it. E.g., kasa, to bite. (Root kas-.) kasite, it bit. kasinari, a thing that bites. Usually the stress is slight and the other syllables follow evenly without accentuation. But occasionally in speech the stress is increased remarkably by the vehemence of the speaker or the necessity of expressing different shades of meaning by the same word. E.g., sahtatenju, he beat me . But if the speaker is very sore about it he will em[p]hasise the first syllable sah-, sometimes in extraordinary fashion. ... Occasionally the second syllable and not the root is accented in en[m]phatic statements. new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (initial syllable, rule string 10/100/1000..), adding that stress is non-phonemic (loudness only) and that non-initial long vowels carry extra loudness. Caveat: this is the family-level typology paragraph of ch. 1, applied to Kui only by implication; the Kui-specific ch. 2 suprasegmentals section was not obtainable (listed open copy is a one-page ERIC abstract).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide typological statement (not Kui-specific): stress is never phonemic in any Dravidian language; it normally falls on the initial syllable regardless of that syllable's length; a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels; short vowels in unaccented non-root syllables tend to be lost.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; only the remark that a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the statement is 'normally' and covers the whole family, with no Kui-specific qualification.
new_statements.identity_note: Friend-Pereira 1909 describes Kui of the Kandhmals and Gumsur tracts (it mentions East Kandh Mals, West Kandh Mals and Gumsar dialect variants for consonants) and states the accent rule for Kui in general, with no dialect restriction. Krishnamurti's statement is for the Dravidian family as a whole, not Kui specifically.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's initial-syllable pattern: the accent is on the base syllable, which in a prefixless, suffixing language is the initial syllable (the example gī-ppk-i-nenju has the accent on the first syllable). The source states the rule morphologically (root/base) rather than positionally, and explicitly frames it as the general Dravidian pattern; it gives one example and no evidence that root and initial syllable ever diverge.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent sits on the syllable of the base (root) of the word, before any formative or inflexional suffix is added; since Kui words are built by suffixation only, this base syllable is the first syllable of the word (gī- in gī-ppk-i-nenju 'he is doing').
new_statements.exceptions: None. Elsewhere (p. 3, on hardening of the formative and the plural suffix -kka) the author speaks of a hard form used 'to lay particular stress on the word', which is emphasis, not word-stress placement.
new_statements.identity_note: Friend-Pereira 1909 describes Kui of the Kandhmals and Gumsur tracts (it mentions East Kandh Mals, West Kandh Mals and Gumsar dialect variants for consonants) and states the accent rule for Kui in general, with no dialect restriction. Krishnamurti's statement is for the Dravidian family as a whole, not Kui specifically.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement. Friend-Pereira 1909 (Kui-specific) puts the accent on the base/root syllable of the word before suffixation; Krishnamurti 2003 (family-wide, from the on-disk ch. 1 typology paragraph) puts non-phonemic stress on the initial syllable. In Kui, a purely suffixing language, the root syllable is the initial syllable, so the two formulations pick out the same syllable and both match the catalog's initial-stress rule string. The only nuance is that Krishnamurti calls stress non-phonemic and notes extra loudness on non-initial long vowels, and Winfield 1928 (already held by the project from the dawi1234 check, not in this works list) adds that emphasis can shift stress to a non-root syllable; neither contradicts the initial/root placement.
